chapters.title: Chapter 1: What Commodities Are and Why They Trade

lessons.title: What Is a Commodity? Hard vs Soft, Standardisation and Why Prices Swing

children.text: In July 2023, tomatoes crossed ₹200 per kg in several Indian cities. Nobody's tomatoes had become tastier. Heat and pest damage in key growing areas, followed by heavy monsoon rains that disrupted supply, turned a cheap kitchen staple into a headline. Gold, crude oil, jeera and copper move for the same basic reason: supply and demand for a physical good that is essentially the same no matter who produces it. By the end of this lesson you will know what makes something a commodity, the families commodities fall into, why exchanges insist on standard contracts, and why commodity prices swing harder than most people expect.

body.text: A commodity is a raw material where one unit is as good as any other unit of the same grade. Because buyers do not care who produced it, price is the only thing left to compete on, and price is set by supply and demand.

children.text: What Makes Something a Commodity

markDefs.definition: Interchangeable: one unit of a given grade can be replaced by any other unit of the same grade without any loss of value.

children.text: A commodity is a basic good, usually a raw material or a primary farm product, that is
fungible
: one unit of a given grade can be swapped for any other unit of the same grade and nobody loses out.
Test it against things you already know:
A 10 gram bar of 24 karat gold. Commodity.
Whether it was refined in Switzerland or in Gujarat, a buyer pays for weight and purity.
A barrel of Brent crude. Commodity.
Refiners buy on grade and delivery terms, not on which rig pumped it.

markDefs.definition: A unit of weight equal to 100 kg, widely used for agricultural produce in Indian mandis and on NCDEX.

children.text: A quintal of graded jeera from Unjha. Commodity.
Buyers pay for a defined quality, not a particular farm. A
quintal
is 100 kg.
A share of Reliance Industries. Not a commodity.
Its value depends on one company's businesses, management and profits.
An M.F. Husain painting. Not a commodity.
Each one is unique, and the artist is the whole point.

body.title: Owning a share vs owning a commodity

columns.label: Owning a share
points: A claim on a business and its profits
Value can compound as the company grows
Driven mainly by one company's performance

columns.label: Owning a commodity
points: A claim on a physical good, with no profits behind it
Pays no dividend or interest, and storage and insurance can cost you
A kilogram stays a kilogram; it does not grow
Driven by global supply and demand, weather, geopolitics and currency

body.text: This is the biggest mindset shift for equity investors. A good company can grow its earnings for 20 years. A kilogram of gold will still be a kilogram of gold in 20 years. Commodity returns come from price changes alone, so every commodity position is, in some form, a call on supply and demand.

children.text: The Families of Commodities: Hard and Soft
The oldest split is by how a commodity comes into existence.
Hard commodities
are mined or extracted from the earth.
Soft commodities
are grown. Traders then break these into four working groups.

body.caption: The main commodity groups, with examples that trade in India

cells: Jeera, guar seed, turmeric, coriander, castor seed, cotton

children.text: Why does the split matter? Because it tells you what drives supply. Hard commodities depend on mines, wells and refineries that take years and thousands of crores to build. Soft commodities depend on sowing decisions, the monsoon and pests, and their supply resets every season.

body.title: Hard or soft?
body.question: Which of these is a soft commodity?
body.explanation: Jeera is grown, which makes it a soft commodity. Copper and silver are mined and natural gas is extracted, so all three are hard commodities.

children.text: Standardisation: Why Exchanges Define Every Detail

markDefs.definition: The exchange document that fixes a contract's quality, lot size, price quotation, trading hours, expiry and settlement or delivery terms.

children.text: Fungibility is what lets a commodity trade on an exchange. But "gold" or "jeera" is too vague for a contract. Is the gold 22 karat or 24? Is the jeera clean, or full of stones and dust? So exchanges like MCX and NCDEX publish a
contract specification
that fixes every detail in advance: quality, quantity per lot, price quotation, and how settlement or delivery happens. Buyers and sellers are left to agree on just one thing: price.

body.caption: What a contract fixes: MCX examples (specifications can change, so always check the exchange website)

body.label: Quote unit vs lot size
body.value: Gold trades in 1 kg lots but is quoted per 10 grams
body.context: At ₹1,00,000 per 10 grams, one 1 kg lot is worth ₹1 crore, because 1 kg is 100 times 10 grams.

body.title: The defining property
body.textWithBlank: Because one unit of a given grade can replace any other unit of that grade, a commodity is described as ___.
body.explanation: Fungibility is what makes standard exchange contracts possible. If every unit were different, like paintings, there would be nothing standard to trade.

body.text: Standardisation applies to exchange contracts, not to your neighbourhood jeweller. A 22 karat necklace is not an MCX gold contract, and its price includes making charges and GST on top of the metal value. Always compare like with like.

children.text: Why Commodity Prices Swing So Hard

markDefs.definition: When the quantity supplied or demanded barely changes even though the price changes a lot, usually because producers and users cannot adjust quickly.

children.text: Many commodities, crude oil and farm products especially, swing harder than the Nifty 50. The reason is that in the short run both supply and demand are stubborn, or
price inelastic

. A farmer cannot grow more cotton mid-season because prices rose. A refinery cannot stop needing crude because prices doubled. When neither side can adjust quickly, even a small shortage forces price to do all the adjusting.
Five forces do most of the damage:
Weather and the monsoon.
A weak or erratic monsoon hurts kharif sowing of cotton, guar and soybean. Unseasonal rain near harvest can damage rabi crops like jeera.
Geopolitics and supply decisions.
Wars, sanctions and OPEC+ production cuts can move crude oil within hours.
The global economy.
Copper and aluminium go into wiring, construction, vehicles and power grids, so their prices track global growth, especially China's.
The rupee.
Gold, silver, crude and base metals are priced globally in US dollars. When the rupee weakens, their price in India rises even if the global price does not move.
Government policy.
Export bans, import duties and stock limits can reshape prices overnight. India banned onion exports in December 2023 to cool domestic prices and lifted the ban in May 2024.

body.caption: Before import duty and GST. 1 troy ounce = 31.1035 grams.

body.title: Show me the math: the rupee moves, gold does not

markDefs.definition: The standard unit for pricing precious metals globally, equal to 31.1035 grams. It is heavier than an ordinary ounce of 28.35 grams.

children.text: Say international gold is at $3,000 per
troy ounce
and USD/INR is 85. These are illustrative numbers, not today's prices.
Price per gram in dollars: 3,000 ÷ 31.1035 = $96.45
Price per 10 grams: $964.52
Now the rupee weakens to 88 and global gold does not move at all: 964.52 × 88 = ₹84,878. Indian gold is up about ₹2,894, or roughly 3.5%, purely because of the currency.

body.title: The rupee strengthens
body.prompt: International gold stays at $3,000 per troy ounce, but USD/INR moves from 85 to 83. Using the formula above, what is the new Indian gold price per 10 grams before duty and GST, rounded to the nearest rupee?
body.explanation: 3,000 ÷ 31.1035 × 10 = $964.52. Multiply by 83 to get about ₹80,055. A ₹2 move in the rupee cut the Indian price by about ₹1,929, around 2.4%, with no change in global gold.

children.text: A Real Swing: The Guar Seed Mania of 2011 and 2012

Guar is a hardy kharif crop grown mostly in Rajasthan's dry districts, and for decades it was an unglamorous commodity. Then the US shale boom arrived. Guar gum, made from the seed, thickens the fluids pumped into shale wells during hydraulic fracturing, and India grows most of the world's guar. Demand from American drillers surged, and farmers could not produce more until the next harvest. That is the textbook recipe for an inelastic price spike.

body.title: Guar seed: from boom to bust

events.title: Shale demand surges
events.description: US fracking activity triggers a rush for guar gum, while Indian supply is fixed until the next harvest.

events.title: Prices multiply
events.description: NCDEX guar seed prices rise several times over in a matter of months.

events.title: The regulator steps in
events.description: The Forward Markets Commission, then the commodity market regulator, moves to curb speculation, and guar futures trading on NCDEX is suspended.

events.title: Planting jumps
events.description: Drawn by record prices, farmers sharply expand guar acreage.

events.title: The bust
events.description: As supply caught up and shale drilling slowed with the 2014 to 2015 oil price crash, guar prices fell far below their peak.

events.title: FMC merges with SEBI
events.description: Commodity derivatives come under SEBI's regulation.

body.text: Notice the full cycle: a demand shock, a price spike because supply cannot respond, a planting rush, then a glut and a crash. In commodities, high prices are often the cure for high prices. You will see this pattern again in jeera, cotton and even crude oil.

body.title: Is it really a commodity bet?
body.scenario: Priya, a 29-year-old software engineer in Hyderabad, has ₹2 lakh to invest. One colleague says, "Buy Coal India shares, it's a commodity play." Another suggests a gold ETF. Her uncle wants her to buy 50 kg of jeera from a trader he knows and store it at home until prices rise.
body.prompt: For each option, is Priya actually getting commodity exposure? What would drive her returns, and what practical problems could she face?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Coal India shares: not a commodity. She would own part of a company. Coal prices matter, but so do production volumes, costs, government pricing decisions, dividends and management. At best this is indirect commodity exposure.
2. Gold ETF: fairly direct exposure to the rupee price of gold, held in her demat account and backed by physical gold, with no storage worry. She pays an expense ratio.
3. 50 kg of jeera at home: direct physical exposure, with real problems. She cannot easily verify quality, she pays the trader's margin to buy and will likely take a discount to sell, home storage risks moisture and pests, and there is no transparent price to sell at. Exchange contracts exist precisely to solve these problems.

body.title: Spot the commodities around you this week
steps: Note the gold rate per 10 grams at a jeweller or on a jewellery website, and check whether it is for 22 or 24 karat.
Check the petrol price in your city and ask why it barely moved while global crude moved.
Look up one commodity on the MCX website and note the unit it is quoted in.
Compare onion or tomato prices at your local market today with a month ago.

cards.definition: A fungible raw material or primary product whose price is set by supply and demand, not by who produced it.
Interchangeable: any unit of a given grade can replace any other unit of the same grade.
A commodity that is mined or extracted, such as gold, copper or crude oil.
A commodity that is grown, such as jeera, guar seed or cotton.
The exchange rulebook for a contract: quality, lot size, quotation, expiry and settlement.
Supply or demand that barely responds to price in the short run, which makes prices swing harder.
The global pricing unit for precious metals, equal to 31.1035 grams.

points: A commodity is a fungible raw material, so its price is set by supply and demand, not by who produced it.
Owning a commodity gives you no earnings or dividends. Returns come only from price changes.
Hard commodities (metals and energy) are mined or extracted. Soft commodities (agri) are grown.
Exchanges like MCX and NCDEX standardise quality, lot size and quotation so that only price is negotiated.
Prices swing hard because short-run supply and demand are inelastic. Weather, geopolitics, growth, the rupee and policy are the main triggers.
High prices often cure themselves by pulling in new supply, as guar seed showed in 2012.
